title: Tap a beer keg with a Sankey D coupler
instruction: Tap the keg with the coupler.
context: Changing kegs is routine bar work: the coupler goes onto the keg's Sankey valve, turns a quarter turn under the valve's lugs, and only then is the handle pushed down, which drives the probe into the valve and opens it. Pressing the handle first pushes the probe into an unlocked coupler, which on a pressurised keg blows it off and sprays beer. Done by bartenders (O*NET 35-3011.00; 711,140 US jobs in BLS OEWS May 2023), who change kegs on shift, and barbacks (35-9011.00, dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers, 483,390).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left); heights above the counter top. Keg: a sixtel (26 kg) of which only the top is modelled, standing free on the counter centred at x 28, y 0: a 23 cm stainless 12-sided top plate 1.2 cm up, a 4 mm chime ring round its edge 4 cm tall, and in the middle the Sankey D valve neck, a 3.4 cm octagon rising 1.6 cm above the plate (top 2.8 cm up) with two dark bayonet lugs on its left and right faces. Drip tray: fixed black block 10 x 10 x 0.8 cm at x 28, y -20. Coupler: chrome Sankey D coupler, 0.9 kg in all, standing on the tray: a 6.4 cm square base with a 6 mm skirt (5.6 cm inside) that fits over the valve neck, orange bayonet ears on its left and right, a 4.6 cm square body 4.6 cm tall, a black beer outlet 1.6 cm square on top (2.5 cm tall) and a dark gas inlet on its far side. Its handle (8 cm chrome bar with a black grip, 100 g) is pivoted on the body's near side 4.4 cm above the base, pointing toward the robot, raised 35 deg; it turns down 60 deg to a stop, on a spring that holds it up until the bar passes horizontal (over centre) and holds it down after. Inside, a probe (50 g) is cammed by the handle 11.5 mm down into the valve.
scoring: From the episode's recorded poses (the trial video on a real rig). Caught: the coupler set on the valve neck within 5 mm of its axis, upright within 5 deg, ears within 10 deg of the lugs; it then turns only about the valve, clockwise seen from above, to a stop at 90 deg. Score 0, latched for the episode, if the handle is pushed more than 30 deg down while the coupler is turned less than 80 deg, if the keg moves more than 10 mm or tilts more than 5 deg, or if the coupler is knocked over (tilted more than 30 deg) or put down on the bare counter; also 0 if the coupler never caught. Otherwise the sum of: coupler turned 85 deg or more 0.3; handle locked over centre (52 deg or more down) 0.4; probe 90% or more of its travel into the valve 0.2; turned 85 deg or more, with no gripper within 2 cm of the coupler or handle and both still, for 1 s 0.1. Success at 1.0 held 1 s. Scored at the last step.
reset_notes: Lift the handle back up past centre, turn the coupler back 90 deg and lift it off the valve, stand it on the drip tray with the handle pointing at the robot, and set the keg on its outline with the lugs left and right.
fidelity: Rigid boxes, one shared friction; the keg is cut to its top 4 cm but carries a full sixtel's 26 kg. The bayonet lugs are a joint, not geometry: the coupler catches when seated within 5 mm and 10 deg of the lug line and then turns 0-90 deg on a revolute. Handle over-centre is a spring whose rest point flips at horizontal; the probe is a sprung slider cammed by the handle. No beer or CO2 pressure is simulated; forcing the handle early latches 0.
